summary: Mars is on average 140 million miles from Earth, so a message takes 3 to 22 minutes each way and the link can drop for about two weeks around solar conjunction. The crew cannot count on a flight surgeon answering in real time. Sonnenblume is a working, offline web app that treats distance from Earth as a medical input. Each day a crew member logs up to 12 indicators from simple instruments (heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood, exercise, fluids, dosimeter, a vision check and weekly mass). A Rust status engine compiled to WebAssembly rates every reading Nominal, Watch or Act now, flags sudden changes from the person's own baseline and shows the result on a male or female anatomical body map. Advice, crew alerts and the Earth outbox change with the communication delay. A Mind tab screens mental health with PHQ-9 and GAD-7, and a Crew ops tab gives the medical officer the whole crew, EVA readiness and a compact report for Earth. Triage, 85 protocols, 139 medicines with label-sourced doses checked against vital signs, and an onboard pharmacy support the crew while Earth is out of reach. It targets NASA's Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes Due to In-flight Medical Conditions and supports Earth-Independent Medical Operations. On Earth it fits Antarctic crews, analog habitats and remote communities.
details:
What it does and how it works

Sonnenblume (German for sunflower) is a crew self-health console for long-duration missions. It is built for the moment when the crew has to be its own first responder. Live app: https://aegis-crew-health.vercel.app (console: /app.html). It opens with 31 days of demo data so anyone can try it.

1. Choose the mission. The crew picks one of five environments: space station, deep-space transit, lunar surface base, pressurised lunar rover or Mars surface base. This sets the typical daily radiation rate, the mission length and the one-way delay to Earth.

2. Log the day. The Log tab records 12 indicators: resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen (SpO2), temperature, fasting blood sugar, sleep, mood, exercise, fluid intake, dosimeter reading, a vision check (near-vision card and Amsler grid, for SANS) and weekly body mass, plus a symptom checklist. Values are typed in by hand. Each field shows its normal range while the user types.

3. Understand the result. A status engine written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly rates every reading Nominal, Watch or Act now against general adult clinical reference ranges (for example, SpO2 below 92% is Act now). Three extra checks catch what a single number misses: a sudden change from the crew member's own baseline or between two readings on the same day, a rebound from an Act now value within 24 hours, and critical readings outside a plausible range, which may be a loose sensor or an emergency. Some rules look across days, for example sleep under 6 hours for three nights in a row.

4. See it on the body. An anatomical body map, drawn in code as SVG, has male and female versions and organ and bone layers. Nine body systems (brain and behaviour, eyes, heart and vessels, lungs and cabin air, digestion and kidneys, muscles, bones and spine, immune system, and a radiation aura) glow by status. Tapping one explains what it does, how spaceflight affects it and what to do now.

5. Act. "What to do now" lists plain steps for every flagged indicator. The advice depends on distance: near Earth it says contact the flight surgeon; with a long delay it says start the onboard protocol with the crew medical officer first.

6. Escalate. When two or more indicators reach Act now, the app automatically posts a crew alert for the crew leader and medical officer to a simulated crew net, and posts a follow-up when fewer than two remain at Act now. Any crew member can also press "Alert now". For deep-space transit and Mars, the user sets a one-way delay of 1 to 22 minutes (Mars is about 3 to 22 minutes) or a solar conjunction blackout. Earth-independent mode switches on at a delay of 5 minutes or more, or during a blackout. An outbox shows when each message reaches Earth, and messages queue during a blackout and are released when the link returns. A status report for the flight surgeon is about 1 KB, small enough for a weak link.

7. "I feel unwell" triage. A crew member ticks symptoms from a list of 30. The app gives an urgency level (Act now, Same day or Self-care), opens the matching protocol, can add the symptoms to today's log, and offers a crew alert for the most serious ones.

8. Medical library. 322 records: 139 medicines (with links to the official DailyMed label and MedlinePlus), 85 guided protocols (24 rated critical), 18 procedure guides such as CPR in microgravity, splinting and building a storm shelter, plus conditions, countermeasures, radiation shielding, radiation events and sources. A protocol can be run as a checklist: each step is timestamped and the finished log goes to the simulated crew and Earth outbox.

9. Onboard pharmacy and dose check. The pharmacy tracks stock and flags medicines that are expired, low or will expire before the mission ends. Before a medicine is given, the dose check reads the latest vital signs and blocks or warns: for example, no sedating medicine when SpO2 is below 92%, and no heart-slowing medicine when the heart rate is below 60. Dose numbers are never invented: 100 medicines carry an adult dose reference traced to the official FDA label on DailyMed and confirmed by a second source (MedlinePlus or NHS); if they disagree the safer value is used, and a number that cannot be confirmed is not shown. Each reference links its sources and adds kidney, liver and older-adult notes. The flight surgeon's own dose table always takes priority.

10. Space weather and radiation. A small server function pulls the last 30 days of solar flares, solar energetic particle events and geomagnetic storms from NASA DONKI. It rates current solar activity: an X-class flare in the last 48 hours or a solar particle event in the last 72 hours is Act now, and an M-class flare in the last 48 hours is Watch. The panel links to the storm shelter guide and the solar particle event protocol. A radiation budget tracks the cumulative dose against the 600 mSv career limit in NASA-STD-3001.

11. Mind (mental health). A 30-second daily check-in (stress, energy, sleep quality, connection to crew and home) is compared with the person's own baseline. Weekly PHQ-9 and GAD-7 screens use the standard public-domain wording; a risky answer or worrying journal words open a safety card with a one-tap alert to the crew medical officer. An isolation tracker, breathing and grounding tools and a private on-device journal complete it.

12. Crew ops. A medical officer view shows every crew member's indicators at a glance; EVA and task readiness gives Go, Caution or No-go with every rule that fired (vitals, sleep, symptoms, sedating medicine, live space weather); a countermeasure planner adapts exercise, fluids and sleep to the mission and the person's trends; and a 7-day handover report of about 750 bytes goes to Earth through the comms delay.

13. Trends and routine. Day, week and month charts show each numeric indicator over time. A daily routine with XP, streaks and badges keeps the logging habit going.

14. Offline, backup and privacy. The app installs as a progressive web app and works offline. All data stays in the browser. The user can export a report or the full JSON record, download and restore a backup file, or delete everything from the Privacy page.

How it is creative

- The comms delay is part of the logic, not just a label. Advice, alerts and the outbox all change with distance, including a solar conjunction blackout that queues messages until the link returns.

- It does not trust good news blindly: a reading that jumps back from Act now to normal within 24 hours is marked Watch, because a sudden recovery can mean a sensor fault or an unstable patient.

- The body map is the dashboard: status is shown on the organ or bone it belongs to, in male and female versions, with radiation as an aura around the body.

- Safety comes from the crew's own data: the dose check reads today's vital signs before any medicine, and the triage connects a symptom straight to a protocol.

- Medicine supply is planned against the mission calendar, not just the shelf: the pharmacy flags every medicine that will expire before the mission's end date, a known problem for exploration formularies (Diaz et al., 2024).

- Live NASA DONKI data becomes a crew instruction: a solar particle event in the last 72 hours or an X-class flare in the last 48 hours turns the space weather panel to Act now, with direct links to the storm shelter guide and the solar particle event protocol.

- The daily routine follows the crew day (morning vitals, midday exercise, evening vision card and dosimeter) and pays a perfect-day bonus, because trends and sudden-change checks only work when the log is complete.

Benefits

- One place for the daily picture: 12 indicators, symptoms, body map, trends and alerts, without the user having to interpret raw numbers.

- Catches patterns, not only bad values: sudden swings, rebounds, implausible readings and multi-day trends.

- Guidance that fits the distance from Earth, so the crew knows when to act on its own.

- Safer medicine use: vital-sign checks before a dose, and no invented dose numbers.

- Supply awareness for missions without resupply: stock and expiry against the mission end date.

- Works with no network and very little bandwidth, and keeps health data private.

Intended impact

NASA's Earth-Independent Medical Operations work describes crews that must handle medical care without real-time help from Earth. Sonnenblume shows how that can look at the level of a single crew member: a short daily routine (12 indicators and a symptom checklist) that turns measurements into clear decisions and brings the crew medical officer in early. For the ground team it produces a short, structured record that survives long delays. On Earth, the same approach fits places where a doctor is far away: Antarctic and polar stations, analog habitats, ships and remote communities, and training for future crews. Next step: try the routine with an analog or training crew and measure how many days are logged, how long each log takes, and how often a Watch or Act now flag leads to an early check by the medical officer.

Tools, languages and technologies

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no build step, so it runs in any modern browser.

- Rust (rust/core) for the status engine: vital-sign thresholds, critical values, personal-baseline shift detection and the radiation budget, compiled to a 2 KB WebAssembly file. The console falls back to identical JavaScript rules if WebAssembly is unavailable, and a test sweeps thousands of values to prove both agree. Cargo unit tests run in CI.

- SVG for the procedural anatomy (js/body.js) and HTML canvas for the trend charts.

- Service worker and web app manifest for offline use.

- Vercel hosting and two Node.js serverless functions: one proxies NASA DONKI (api.nasa.gov) with a one-hour cache, the other optionally reads the medical library from Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB and falls back to the bundled JSON files.

- Strict Content Security Policy and security headers, self-hosted fonts, and validation of all stored data.

- Python and Playwright browser tests (112 checks), Rust unit tests, an axe-core accessibility scan and GitHub Actions on every push.

- Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant during development (see Use of AI). The app itself runs no AI model.

Factors we considered

Privacy: health data never leaves the browser unless the user exports it. The app sends no personal data to any server, the security policy allows connections only to its own domain, and a Privacy Charter page explains this and lets the user delete all data.

Scientific validity: the choice of indicators and the spaceflight explanations come from NASA Human Research Program evidence reports and NASA-STD-3001 (listed under NASA data), which also gives the 600 mSv career radiation limit. The Nominal, Watch and Act now thresholds are general adult clinical reference ranges, not NASA limits and not individual medical limits. Radiation rates are approximate published figures for the ISS, Mars cruise and surface (Zeitlin 2013, Hassler 2014) and the lunar surface (Zhang 2020).

Safety: the app never replaces the crew medical officer or flight surgeon; every Act now path ends with a person. Critical readings first ask the user to check the sensor. Medicine doses are never invented: numbers come only from the flight surgeon's dose table or from label references confirmed by two sources, and the dose check can block a medicine from today's vital signs. Stored data is treated as untrusted and validated, damaged data is recovered from a rolling backup, and an error in one panel cannot take down the rest of the console.

Honest limits: this is a student prototype and not a medical device. It uses demo data and manual input, not real sensors. Crew alerts, reports and protocol logs are simulated inside the browser. Pharmacy shelf lives are illustrative. The library text is educational demo content and is not clinically validated. Live space weather needs a connection and can fall back to NASA's shared demo API key, which has rate limits. Data on a lost device is gone unless the user has a backup.

Use of AI (SI)

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant, following the NASA Space Apps rules on Super Intelligence:

- Code: the web app, Rust status engine, body map, serverless functions, service worker, tests and CI setup were written and debugged with Claude.

- Library text: the medicines, protocols, guides and other library entries were drafted with Claude from public sources and reviewed by the team. They are educational demo content, not medical guidance.

- Presentation: Claude drafted slides 4 to 6 of the demo deck (Mind, Crew ops, medicine doses) and helped word this project page; the team reviewed them.

- Images: any AI-generated image we use carries a visible "AI-generated image (SI)" watermark.

The team chose the problem, scope, design and sources, directed the work and reviewed the results. The app itself contains no AI, and no personal or health data is ever sent to an AI service. The AI disclosure is also shown in the site footer, page metadata and README.
